title: Medellín: El Poblado and Provenza
summary: From the metro by the river, through old Manila and the square where El Poblado began, to Parque Lleras, the La Octava ball-pit bar, El Social and the designer shops and cafés of Vía Primavera.
intro: Welcome to El Poblado! Today this is Medellín's most international neighbourhood, full of trees, cafés, restaurants and bars. But it's also where the story of the city began, more than four hundred years ago. This walk takes about two hours, starting at the Poblado metro station and climbing gently through the neighbourhood to Provenza. There are plenty of chances to stop for a coffee, a juice or something to eat, so take your time. Keep your phone in your pocket between stops, and let's go.

stops.name: Poblado Metro Station
stops.text: We start at the corner of Poblado station, on Line A of the Medellín Metro. Opened in 1995, it is still the only metro in Colombia, and people here are very proud of it. Notice how clean it is: no graffiti, no litter. Locals call this respect for shared spaces cultura metro, metro culture. Line A runs along the Medellín River, right at the bottom of the valley. From here we walk uphill, east, toward the mountains. Across Calle 10, to your left, is the Centro Comercial Monterrey, Medellín's famous tech mall: floor after floor of small shops selling, and fixing, computers, phones and gadgets. It has been here for decades, and locals still go there to hunt for a good deal. Now walk east along Calle 10, and cross the big avenues only at the traffic lights.
stops.credit: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Across Avenida Las Vegas
stops.text: At Avenida Las Vegas, cross at the lights, then bear left toward Calle 11. Somewhere under your feet, the La Presidenta stream is finishing its trip down the hill into the river. We'll meet the same stream later, up in a green park.

stops.name: Onto Calle 11
stops.text: Keep going east along Calle 11. The flat valley floor behind you is a tangle of avenues, rails and the river; from here the city starts to climb. On your right, across Calle 10, is the Éxito of El Poblado, another place that has been here for decades. Éxito is Colombia's biggest supermarket chain, and it was born right here in Medellín, in 1949.

stops.name: Left onto Carrera 43F
stops.text: Turn left onto Carrera 43F, a quiet street of low houses. You're entering Manila.

stops.name: Right onto Calle 11A
stops.text: Turn right onto Calle 11A and walk a few steps.

stops.name: Manila
stops.text: Welcome to Manila, one of the oldest residential corners of El Poblado. Look at the scale of it: two- and three-storey houses, a tight grid of streets, trees, and almost no towers. Many of these old family homes are now cafés, small restaurants, hostels and co-working spaces, which gives the neighbourhood a young, relaxed feel. Nearby there's even a public skate park, busy in the afternoons. It's a good place to see how El Poblado looked before the high-rises arrived. Now keep walking east along Calle 11A.

stops.name: Onto Calle 11
stops.text: Where Calle 11A ends, keep right onto Calle 11 and walk east for one short block.

stops.name: Right onto Carrera 43C
stops.text: Turn right onto Carrera 43C and walk downhill.

stops.name: Carrera 43C bars
stops.text: This little street, Carrera 43C, has two places we really like, almost side by side: Siete Pulgadas, a listening bar, and Mad Records Café. Both names point to music: seven inches, siete pulgadas, is the size of a vinyl single. A listening bar is a place built around a great sound system, where people come to really listen to the music while they have a drink. If it's evening, this is a great place to come back to. For now, keep walking down Carrera 43C to Calle 10.

stops.name: Left onto Calle 10
stops.text: At the bottom, turn left onto Calle 10 and walk one block east.

stops.name: Milla de Oro
stops.text: One block ahead runs Avenida El Poblado, also called Carrera 43A. For most of the twentieth century this area was countryside: big country houses, called fincas, where wealthy families from downtown came to escape the city. As Medellín grew, the fincas were replaced by apartment towers, hotels and offices, and the stretch of the avenue further south became known as the Milla de Oro, the Golden Mile, for its banks and business headquarters. Now cross Calle 10 at the crosswalk and walk down Carrera 43B, beside the park, to its lower corner.

stops.name: El Poblado Park
stops.text: You're standing where Medellín began. In 1616, a Spanish colonial official, Francisco de Herrera Campuzano, set up a settlement for the indigenous people of the valley right here, called San Lorenzo de Aburrá. That's why this neighbourhood is called El Poblado, the settlement. The town of Medellín itself grew up later, further north, where the Centro is today. Look around at the mountains on every side. Medellín sits in a long, narrow valley, at about fifteen hundred metres, and the temperature stays pleasant all year. That's why it's called the City of Eternal Spring. From this lower corner, look down Carrera 43B: a pedestrian street full of bars and restaurants, busy from lunchtime until late at night. And right on the park is Alambique, a restaurant we love. Ask for the ceviche de chicharrón, a new fusion version of ceviche made with crispy pork. When you're ready, walk east along Calle 9, along the bottom of the park, to Carrera 43A.

stops.name: Cross at the light
stops.text: At Carrera 43A, wait for the green light and cross at the crosswalk.

stops.name: Church side
stops.text: Once across, turn left and walk a few steps up to the church.

stops.name: San José del Poblado Church
stops.text: This is the church of San José del Poblado, the parish church of the neighbourhood. Look up at its tall brick tower with the clock. Like in almost every Colombian town, the square and the church go together: for centuries this was where people met after Sunday mass, did business and caught up on news. El Poblado has changed completely around it, but the plaza and its church are still the heart of the old village. If the doors are open, step inside for a quiet moment. Next to the church, along Carrera 43A, look for the little hot dog stands. Perritos calientes are a classic of this park: they're tiny, so you can easily eat a few. Then, staying on this side of the avenue, walk south along Carrera 43A, past the hot dog stands, toward the green park by the stream.
stops.place: Parroquia San José del Poblado Medellín

stops.name: South on Carrera 43A
stops.text: Walk south along the sidewalk of Carrera 43A, Avenida El Poblado, for about two blocks, then turn left onto Calle 8.

stops.name: Café Zorba
stops.text: Here on Calle 8, right by the park, is Café Zorba, one of our favourite spots in El Poblado. It's a vegetarian place, and they make very good pizza: a great stop for a coffee or a bite before the green part of the walk. When you're ready, keep following Calle 8 as it turns into a path and goes down into the park.

stops.name: Down into the park
stops.text: Follow the path down into the park, toward the stream.

stops.name: Left along the stream
stops.text: At the bottom, turn left onto the path along the stream. It's suddenly much quieter here.

stops.name: La Presidenta Linear Park
stops.text: This green strip follows the La Presidenta stream down the hill, the same stream you crossed near the metro. Medellín is crossed by hundreds of streams like this one, all flowing into the river at the bottom of the valley. In recent years the city has been turning streets and streams into green corridors, planting thousands of trees and plants to cool the city down, and it won international awards for it. Listen for the birds. You might see bright green parakeets, or the noisy, yellow-chested bird locals call the bichofué. Now follow the path east, along the stream.
stops.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Along the stream
stops.text: Keep following the path east, along the stream. Medellín's streams flood fast in heavy rain, which is why many of them run in deep channels like this one.

stops.name: Path turns right
stops.text: Here the path turns right. Follow it down to the end of the park.

stops.name: Out of the park
stops.text: At the end of the park, turn left and walk out to Carrera 39.

stops.name: Left onto Carrera 39
stops.text: Turn left onto Carrera 39 and walk up half a block.

stops.name: Right onto Calle 8
stops.text: At Calle 8, turn sharp right and walk downhill. Look for a bar on this street.

stops.name: La Octava
stops.text: This is La Octava, one of the most famous bars in El Poblado, and a little crazy. Its best-known feature is a ball pit, a piscina de pelotas, like the ones in children's play areas, except this one is for grown-ups, who jump in with a drink in hand. The house shot has a cheeky name: the Russian cocaine. Relax, it's just a drink, and the name is a joke. The bar comes alive at night, so if you like what you see, come back later. And like everywhere in the nightlife zone: drink at your own pace, and never leave your glass alone. Now walk up Carrera 38, toward Parque Lleras.

stops.name: Up Carrera 38
stops.text: Walk up Carrera 38 to Calle 9; the park is right ahead. We're in the Zona Rosa, the nightlife district: calm by day, packed by night. A few honest tips for going out in Medellín. Use ride apps, or taxis that a restaurant or bar calls for you. Don't accept drinks from strangers. And be careful when meeting people from dating apps.

stops.name: Parque Lleras
stops.text: This is Parque Lleras, the heart of El Poblado's nightlife. Around this small, leafy park are dozens of bars, clubs and restaurants, and on weekend nights it fills with locals and travellers from all over the world. Medellín's music is everywhere: reggaetón, of course, but also salsa, vallenato and electronic music. If you want to learn a few dance steps, many places offer salsa classes for beginners. Now walk up Carrera 38, toward Calle 10.

stops.name: Right onto Calle 10
stops.text: At the top of Carrera 38, turn right onto Calle 10 and walk east, three blocks, to Carrera 35. While you walk, let's talk about food. The classic dish of this region is the bandeja paisa, a huge plate with beans, rice, ground beef, crispy pork belly called chicharrón, a fried egg, sweet plantain, avocado, a little arepa and chorizo. It's a farmer's meal, so share it. For something smaller, try an arepa, or an empanada with spicy ají sauce.

stops.name: Right onto Carrera 35
stops.text: Turn right onto Carrera 35 and walk down it, under the big trees. Look out for fresh fruit juices on the menus here: lulo is tangy and green inside, maracuyá is passion fruit, and guanábana is creamy and sweet.

stops.name: El Social and Coyotaco
stops.text: On this corner is El Social, a tienda mixta, the old-style neighbourhood corner shop, open since 1969. The streets around it filled up with trendy restaurants and bars, but El Social kept its simple tables and its cold beers, and it's a favourite of locals and travellers alike. Stop for a beer and some people-watching: it's a taste of what this neighbourhood was like before. Right next door is Coyotaco, and it comes with a funny story. Coyo Taco started in Miami, created by Colombians, and grew into a chain with places around the world. But it only came to Colombia later, so for years Colombia didn't have Coyotaco, even though its creators were Colombian. When you're ready, keep walking down Carrera 35 to Calle 8.

stops.name: Carolina and 903
stops.text: From this corner, look one block further down Carrera 35. Almost side by side are two places from Medellín's biggest music stars. Carolina is Karol G's restaurant, named after her real name, Carolina Giraldo; she opened it in December 2024, and the menu mixes Colombian cooking and seafood with flavours from across Latin America. Right next to it is 903, Nueve Cero Tres, the nightclub Maluma opened in March 2025, designed to feel like an apartment from the early nineties. Medellín is often called the capital of reggaetón: Karol G, Maluma and J Balvin all come from this city. If you want a closer look, walk down and come back to this corner. Then follow Calle 8 west, toward 37 Park.

stops.name: Along Calle 8
stops.text: Follow Calle 8 as it bends to the right.

stops.name: Calle 8 at Carrera 36
stops.text: At Carrera 36, keep going west along Calle 8. 37 Park is just ahead.

stops.name: 37 Park
stops.text: This is 37 Park, a restaurant and bar here on Calle 8, and another of our recommendations: a good place for a drink or a bite before the last stretch of the walk. Then keep going west along Calle 8 to Carrera 37.

stops.name: Right onto Vía Primavera
stops.text: At Carrera 37, turn right and walk uphill. This street is Vía Primavera.

stops.name: Vía Primavera and Pergamino
stops.text: Carrera 37, Vía Primavera, is the perfect end to our walk. It's lined with small speciality shops, many run by local Colombian designers: clothes, shoes, jewellery and accessories you won't find anywhere else. Medellín is a fashion city, built on the textile industry you hear about on the downtown tour, and every July it hosts Colombiamoda, one of the biggest fashion fairs in Latin America. And right here is Pergamino, one of Medellín's best-known speciality coffee shops. Colombia is one of the world's great coffee countries, and the mountains around Medellín are coffee country too. Sit down, order a coffee, or a tinto, the small black coffee Colombians drink all day long, and rest your feet. In a couple of hours you've gone from the metro by the river, through old Manila, to the square where El Poblado was born four hundred years ago, and up to the streets where Medellín eats, shops and dances today. If you haven't done it yet, the downtown tour tells the other half of the story: how Medellín went from one of the most dangerous cities in the world to one of the most innovative. Thank you for walking with me. Enjoy your coffee, and enjoy Medellín. Gracias, parce.
